rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper reporter questions underneath the launch: "The new enterprise question: which AI agents get write access?" is a real CIO/automation story, not announcement confetti. A's "Airtable just entered the AI agent market - that changes who it competes with" is competent, but it is closer to a standard category wrapper. B still needs a few overclaims trimmed, especially "Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost," but its proof demands and park/advance guidance are more useful to a founder before a reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" overstates one Airtable repositioning into a market-wide conclusion without supplied outside proof.
"Airtable just entered the AI agent market - that changes who it competes with" overlaps with the category angle; category shift and competitive-map are adjacent, not fully separate desks.
"all-in product pivot" is hotter than the facts. The update says repositioning and launch, not company-wide all-in commitment.
It misses the strongest enterprise-operational angle: agents with write access to records, permissions, rollback, and reliability.
gaps_in_B: "Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost" is not grounded. The facts only say Airtable's agent pricing is not finalized.
"Notion, Smartsheet and Monday" are unsupplied competitor names. Plausible, but this exercise is not a memory contest.
"bets the company on agents" is a little too CNBC chyron. The facts support a repositioning, not proof that the whole company is staked on it.
"unusually candid example" decorates the pricing angle. Unfinalized pricing is useful; calling it unusually candid needs evidence.
